Multi-Step Consistency Models: Fast Generation with Theoretical Guarantees

Nishant Jain ††thanks: Equal Contribution Affiliation: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC)    Xunpeng Huang††footnotemark: Affiliation: University of California, San Diego (UCSD)    Yian Ma Affiliation: University of California, San Diego (UCSD)    Tong Zhang Affiliation: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC)
Abstract

Consistency models have recently emerged as a compelling alternative to traditional SDE-based diffusion models, offering a significant acceleration in generation by producing high-quality samples in very few steps. Despite their empirical success, a proper theoretic justification for their speed-up is still lacking. In this work, we provide the analysis which bridges this gap, showing that given a consistency model which can map the input at a given time to arbitrary timestamps along the reverse trajectory, one can achieve KL divergence of order O⁡(ε2)O(\varepsilon^{2}) using only O⁡(log⁡(dε))O\left(\log\left(\frac{d}{\varepsilon}\right)\right) iterations with constant step size, where dd is the data dimension. Additionally, under minimal assumptions on the data distribution—an increasingly common setting in recent diffusion model analyses—we show that a similar KL convergence guarantee can be obtained, with the number of steps scaling as O⁡(d​log⁡(dε))O\left(d\log\left(\frac{d}{\varepsilon}\right)\right). Going further, we also provide a theoretical analysis for estimation of such consistency models, concluding that accurate learning is feasible using small discretization steps, both in smooth and non-smooth settings. Notably, our results for the non-smooth case yield best-in-class convergence rates compared to existing SDE/ODE-based analyses under minimal assumptions.

1 Introduction

Lately, diffusion models [28] have become an important topic of research in computer vision and generative modelling [33, 7, 25, 29, 27, 32, 15], with applications ranging from generating images or videos [10, 6] controllably to other areas like drug/protein design [12, 13]. These models comprise of a forward process which gradually adds noise to the data and then the generation is done by the corresponding denoising process which is also referred to as the reverse/generation process. These forward/reverse processes can either be seen as transition kernels [17, 29, 15] or instead modelled as SDEs [35, 34, 32, 5]. This is popularly referred as score based generative modelling, since the generation process requires a score function which at a given time instant is the gradient of log probability of the marginal distribution corresponding that time.

The generation process of these diffusion based methods is iterative in nature and usually each iteration takes observable time since it requires estimating the score which most commonly is the forward pass through a neural network. This makes the overall process significantly time-consuming for practical applications like generating high resolution images [7, 36] and thus hinders with their applicability in the real world scenarios. A prior work [35] has shown that corresponding to the SDE of the reverse process in the diffusion models, there exists an ODE which also has the same marginals. Thus, it is also possible model the generation process using a deterministic process which corresponds to this reverse ODE. Further developments on these lines led to the discovery of consistency models [31] which exploit this probability flow ODE and learn a single step data generation function from gaussian noise i.e. consistency function.

Since the discovery of these consistency models, there have been works trying to analysis them both theoritically [26, 9, 20] and empirically [18, 30, 14]. The original paper proposed the single step generation function which takes any point along the probability flow ODE to the start i.e. the true data distribution. It also proposed a multi-step sampling scheme utilizing this function with the possibility of further enhancing results. A follow-up work [18] provided an alternative formulation where the consistency function can take from any initial time to any final time along the reverse ODE as against always taking to the start and also proposed an updated training scheme to achieve this. A couple of other works [9, 20] also theoritically analyzed the training of consistency models from a learning theory perspective.

Furthermore, a recent work [26] showed the convergence analysis for these consistency models in the Wassertian distance using the usual assumption on consistency distillation error, score smoothness and score estimation error, but required the step size to be O~​(ϵ2)\tilde{O}(\epsilon^{2}) and thereby showed the discretization complexity comparable to state-of-the-art ODE based methods. In this work, we provide a tighter analysis for multi-step sampling in the KL divergence, which can achieve O⁡(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2}) error with constant step size using the consistency models which, given a sample from some time instant, can generate the corresponding sample at any arbitrary specified time along the reverse probability flow ODE. We provide this analysis for two cases: a) having assumptions similar to the standard assumptions for diffusion based analysis [5, 35, 37] including the previous work on consistency model convergence [26] which includes smoothness of score function, small score estimation error, finite second moment, and b) without assuming that the score function is smooth.

1.1 Related Work

SDE-Based Analysis of Diffusion Models.

The foundational work establishing the effectiveness of diffusion models for generative tasks is the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) framework introduced by [15]. Building on this, [35] demonstrated that the forward noising process in DDPMs can be interpreted as a stochastic differential equation (SDE), laying the groundwork for continuous-time formulations of diffusion models. Subsequent efforts have focused on providing convergence guarantees for such SDE-based generative processes. In particular, [5] presented a convergence analysis under the assumption that the score function is smooth. This line of inquiry was extended by a series of works [21, 20, 19] that further investigated convergence behavior, albeit still relying on various regularity conditions. More recent advancements have relaxed the smoothness assumptions traditionally imposed on the score function. For example, [3] and [2] showed that the generative process can still converge to a Gaussian-perturbed version of the data distribution, even in the absence of score smoothness. Notably, the recent work of [23] achieved an improved convergence rate of 𝒪⁡(d/T)\mathcal{O}(d/T) for DDPM samplers, again without requiring smoothness of the score function.

ODE based diffusion analysis.

Since the discovery of the probability flow ODE, there has been growing interest in deterministic generation for diffusion models. Some prominent works include the DDIM paper [29] which is just the deterministic counterpart of DDPM. A recent work [4] showed under the standard asumptions the ODE also has a provably fast convergence. Convergence analysis of this DDIM sampler has also been discussed in a couple of recent works [22, 11, 16, 21, 24] but require some additional assumptions. The best bounds for a general data distribution requires an assumption on the divergence of the estimated score [22]. A recent work [24] instead exploited the Fokker-Planck equation but again with the additional assumption of Jacobi of estimated score for TV distance analysis. It also shows that without such additional assumptions the TV distance will always be lower bounded by a constant. Another work [11] proposed an analysis in the Wassertian distances but for the strongly log-concave case.

Consistency Model Analysis

The original consistency models paper [31] proposed a single as well multi-step sampling scheme along with distillation based (which requries a pre-trained diffusion model to distill knowledge) and self-consistency training based setups. [26] provides theoritical analysis in the wassertian distance for both single and multi-step sampling, using the score estimation and lipschitz smoothness assumptions, along with the TV error analysis but with additional assumptions. It resulted in the step size/discretization complexity comparable to the state of the art SDE based diffusion. On the training side, a recent work showed how can we achieve consistency trajectory models [18] where the consistency function can take you from any time t1t_{1} to t2t_{2} along the probability flow ODE. Another work [8] exploits the consistency property of diffusion models to mitigate drifts in the data by modifying the de-noising score matching objective in diffusion. Furthermore, a recent work [9] also considered the analysis for consistency diffusion models from a statistical learning theory perspectives and proposed some statistical convergence rates for this based on the Wassertian distance. On similar lines, another work theoretically targeted the number of training steps required for consistency models [20].

2 Preliminaries

Diffusion Models.

Generative modelling via diffusion comprises of two parts. First corresponds to adding noise to the original data distrbution pd​a​t​ap_{data} as a forward process which can be expressed as the following SDE:

d​xt=μ⁡(x,t)​d​t+σ⁡(t)​d​wt,x0∼p0=pd​a​t​a,\displaystyle dx_{t}=\mu(x,t)dt+\sigma(t)dw_{t},\qquad x_{0}\sim p_{0}=p_{data}, (1)

where xt∈ℝdx_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, t∈[0,T]t\in[0,T] where TT is the total time for which we run the noising forward process, μ,σ\mu,\sigma correspond to drift and diffusion coefficients and wtw_{t} corresponds to the Brownian motion, pt=l​a​w​(xt)p_{t}=law(x_{t}) or the marginal distribution of the complete process at a given tt. The corresponding generation process is just a reversal of this SDE:

dxt=[μ(xt,t)−12σ(t)2∇logpt(xt)]dt+g(t)dw¯t.\displaystyle dx_{t}=\left[\mu(x_{t},t)-\frac{1}{2}\sigma(t)^{2}\nabla\log p_{t}(x_{t})\right]dt+g(t)d\bar{w}_{t}. (2)

The corresponding backward probability flow ODE [35] would then be:

dxt=[μ(xt,t)−12σ(t)2∇logpt(xt)]dt,\displaystyle dx_{t}=\left[\mu(x_{t},t)-\frac{1}{2}\sigma(t)^{2}\nabla\log p_{t}(x_{t})\right]dt, (3)

which will have the same marginal as the backward SDE [35] and will start from xT∼pTx_{T}\sim p_{T} in the reverse direction. Using the popular choice of OU process as the forward noising procedure for these diffusion models results in μ⁡(xt,t)=−xt\mu(x_{t},t)=-x_{t}, σ⁡(t)=2\sigma(t)=\sqrt{2}. Solving the SDE results in the following equation for the forward process:

xt=e−t​x0+1−e−2​t​ϵ,ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),x_{t}=e^{-t}x_{0}+\sqrt{1-e^{-2t}}\epsilon,\qquad\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}),

where ptp_{t} is the density of xtx_{t}, with x0∼p0​(x0)=pdata​(x0)x_{0}\sim p_{0}(x_{0})=p_{\text{data}}(x_{0}). Thus, the resultant probability flow ODE becomes:

d​xt=(−xt−st​(xt))​d​t,st​(x)=∇log⁡pt​(x),dx_{t}=\left(-x_{t}-s_{t}(x_{t})\right)dt,\qquad s_{t}(x)=\nabla\log p_{t}(x),

Estimating the score function:

The reverse SDE/probability flow ODE for generation comprises of a term ∇log⁡pt​(xt)\nabla\log p_{t}(x_{t}) which is unknown and is termed as the score function. This is estimated via denoising score matching [33]. Denoting the estimated score function as s^t​(⋅)\hat{s}_{t}(\cdot), it will result in the following probability flow ODE, which is also termed as empirical PF ODE:

d​x^t=(−x^t−s^t​(x^t))​d​td\hat{x}_{t}=\left(-\hat{x}_{t}-\hat{s}_{t}(\hat{x}_{t})\right)dt

where x^t\hat{x}_{t} can be treated as the empirical counterpart of xtx_{t} (and p^t\hat{p}_{t} as the counterpart for ptp_{t} resp. or x^t∼p^t\hat{x}_{t}\sim\hat{p}_{t}) which evolves according to estimated s^t\hat{s}_{t} as against the true score function.

Consistency Models.

For a given process {xt}t∈[δ,T]\{x_{t}\}_{t\in[\delta,T]} following the above probability flow ODE, [31] discussed the existence of a consistency function f⁡(xt,t)f(x_{t},t) as a backward mapping f:ℝd×ℝ+→ℝdf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R^{+}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}, which maps process at any time tt to the start of the trajetcory:

f⁡(xt,t)=xδ∀t∈[δ,T]f(x_{t},t)=x_{\delta}\qquad\forall\,t\in[\delta,T]

learning which can replace the iterative generation process by single step. It is associated to the field v:ℝd×ℝ+→ℝdv:\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R^{+}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} of the corresponding ODE:

d​xt=v⁡(xt,t)​d​tdx_{t}=v(x_{t},t)dt

The paper showed how this model can be learned efficiently by distillation using an ODE solver which will be discussed later in the paper.
Similarly, for the empirical PF ODE discussed above and the associated process {x^t}t∈[δ,T]\{\hat{x}_{t}\}_{t\in[\delta,T]}, we can define the corresponding consistency function as f^​(xt,t)\hat{f}(x_{t},t) where f^​(x^t,t)=x^δ​∀t∈[δ,T]\hat{f}(\hat{x}_{t},t)=\hat{x}_{\delta}\,\forall\,t\in[\delta,T]. Instead of modelling these consistency models as f⁡(xt,t)f(x_{t},t), we will also consider the formulation f⁡(t′,t,xt)f(t^{\prime},t,x_{t}) (and correspondingly f^​(t′,t,x^t)\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,\hat{x}_{t}))where the consistency takes the input at tt to t′<tt^{\prime}<t. Later, we will also provide an error analysis for learning this formulation.

3 Main Results

We will now discuss our convergence results when using the above mentioned formulation of the consistency model. We will consider a multi-step sampling approach using these consistency models and show the convergence of the empirical PF ODE to the true data distribution in the KL divergence. We begin by first defining notations/setup followed by stating the assumptions:

3.2 Multi-step Sampling

We now consider a sequence 0<t0<t1<t2<⋯<tK0<t_{0}<t_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots<t_{K} and let tj′∈[0,tj)t_{j}^{\prime}\in[0,t_{j}). Also, from the notations defined in the previous subsection, law at time tkt_{k} for process 𝐱^t\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t} is denoted as p^tK\hat{p}_{t_{K}} which can also be seen as an approximation of ptKp_{t_{K}} (corresponding to 𝐱tk{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{k}}). Similarly, to keep consistency from the notation above, we will denote the joint of distribution for (𝐱^t0,𝐱^t1,…,𝐱^tK)(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{0}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{1}},...,\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{K}}) (and correspondingly (𝐱t0,𝐱t1,…,𝐱tK)({{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{0}},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{1}},...,{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{K}})) as p^t0,t1,…,tK\hat{p}_{t_{0},t_{1},...,t_{K}} (pt0,t1,…,tK{p}_{t_{0},t_{1},...,t_{K}} respectively). The multi-step sampling using this empirical PF ODE is defined in Algorithm 1. It can be interpreted as first following the empirical PF ODE (eq. 6) to go from time tkt_{k} to some tk−1′t^{\prime}_{k-1} in the reverse (generation) direction and then take a step away (forward) from the generation by adding noise. Figure 1 shows both these steps. This noise can act as a regularizer (smoothener) for the generation process and translates the ODE based generation from the consistency model to some intermediate between ODE and SDE based generation. This, as we will discuss below, leads to better convergence guarantees. Alongside this Algorithm 1, we also define sampling when using the true values in this algorithm (Algorithm 2) which leads to the true data distribution.

We will now consider the convergence of this multi-step sampling Algorithm 1 in the KL divergence w.r.t. true data distribution (or equivalently Algorithm 2) in the subsection below. For clarity, we also define the notation corresponding to the step size corresponding to the above-defined sequences, as hk=tk−tk−1h_{k}=t_{k}-t_{k-1} and hk′=tk−tk−1′h^{\prime}_{k}=t_{k}-t^{\prime}_{k-1}. These can be interpreted as step sizes corresponding to travelling along the reverse trajectory and going back along the forward respectively. Thus, we have the following set of relations:

hk=tk−tk−1<hk′=tk−tk−1′\displaystyle h_{k}=t_{k}-t_{k-1}<h^{\prime}_{k}=t_{k}-t^{\prime}_{k-1} (8)

since based on our definition of the sequence tk′t^{\prime}_{k} above, we will have tk−1′<tk−1t^{\prime}_{k-1}<t_{k-1}.

3.3 Convergence in the KL divergence for multi-step sampling

We first discuss the analysis involving the smoothness assumption, which has also been widely used in the literature [26, 18, 5]. The assumption is as follows:

Assumption 3.3.

The approximate score function 𝐬^t\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t} L−L-Lipschitz with L≥1L\geq 1 for all t≥1t\geq 1.

Notice, that it is a bit different from the previous works since they assume the true score to be L−L-smooth. We provide another analysis where we relax this assumption and incur additional dependence on the dimension dd replacing LL. We now provide our first main result as follows.

Theorem 3.1.

For Algorithm 1, if hk′≤12​(1+L)h^{\prime}_{k}\leq\frac{1}{2(1+L)}, along with assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3 provided, we have:

KL(pt0∥p^t0)≤(d+m2)e−T+e2h′k2εs​c​o​r​e2∑k=1K14​(tk−tk′)\displaystyle KL(p_{t_{0}}\|\hat{p}_{t_{0}})\leq(d+m_{2})e^{-T}+e^{2}{h^{\prime}}_{k}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}_{score}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{4(t_{k}-t^{\prime}_{k})} (9)
Proof.

The complete proof of this theorem is provided in Appendix A. A higher level sketch involves considering the two sources of error: a) Initialization error due to starting the reverse process from a normal distribution (lemma A.5) and b) the error incurred by using empirical PF ODE (eq. 6) instead of the true PF ODE (eq. 5, which will depend on εs​c​o​r​e\varepsilon_{score}). Bounding the first error is straightforward and has been adapted from the existing literature. ∎

Since we know that the total time of the forward process TT would be ∑k=1Khk\sum^{K}_{k=1}h_{k}, we can conclude the following from this theorem:

Corollary 3.2.

Under Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, Algorithm 1 achieves the KL divergence error O⁡(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2}), if we run it for a total time T=log⁡(d+m2ϵ)T=\log(\frac{d+m_{2}}{\epsilon}) with the constant step size say hk=13​(L+1)h_{k}=\frac{1}{3(L+1)} and hk′=12​(L+1)h^{\prime}_{k}=\frac{1}{2(L+1)} (which leads to tk−tk′=hk+1′−hk+1=16​(L+1)t_{k}-t^{\prime}_{k}=h^{\prime}_{k+1}-h_{k+1}=\frac{1}{6(L+1)}), thereby inducing an iteration/discretization complexity K=Thk=3​(L+1)​log⁡(d+m2ϵ)K=\frac{T}{h_{k}}=3(L+1)\log(\frac{d+m_{2}}{\epsilon}) given that the score estimation error from denoising score matching is εs​c​o​r​e=O⁡(ϵl​o​g​(d+m2ϵ))\varepsilon_{score}=O\left(\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{log(\frac{d+m_{2}}{\epsilon})}}\right). Therefore, we can have the step size (and correspondingly the number of iterations) independent (logarithmically dependent) of ϵ\epsilon to achieve O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon) accuracy in the KL divergence which is better then any of the existing results (O⁡(1ϵ))\left(O(\frac{1}{\epsilon})\right) for DDPM [15]/DDIM [29] samplers.

This shows the effectiveness of using the consistency model based formulation for generation tasks with constant step sizes. The best previous works require step size to be atleast O⁡(ϵ)O(\epsilon) for the SDE based generation [23] (thereby inducing an iteration complexyt of O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon})) and require much stricter assumptions for ODE based generation (like the bounded Jacobi) [22, 24]. Also, we can see that this would not be possible to achieve without multi-step sampling, which requires adding noise at each step into the generated samples. This acts as a regularizer and helps to prevent error accumulation. Intuitively, this is similar to what a stochastic differential equation (SDE) achieves in the score-based formulation. Therefore, it is reasonable to conclude that the theoretical advantages of using consistency models become effective when employing the multi-step iterative sampling approach, while requiring far fewer steps compared to standard diffusion-based generation.

We now consider relaxing the assumption 3.3 and provide the convergence in KL for the multi-step sampling in the next subsection.

3.4 Non-Smooth Case

Taking inspiration from recent works [3, 1] on relaxing the smoothness assumption of the true score function, we first define the noise schedule/conditional variance for 𝐱t{\mathbf{x}}_{t} given 𝐱0{\mathbf{x}}_{0} for the forward OU process as σt=1−e−2​t\sigma_{t}=1-e^{-2t} and arrive at the following result for the multi-step sampling (Algorithm 1) in absence of any smoothness.

Theorem 3.3.

For Algorithm 1, using only assumptions 3.1 and 3.2, if we have h′k<σtk−1′2d{h^{\prime}}_{k}<\frac{\sigma^{2}_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}}{d} and the number of iterations K=dσtk−1′2​log⁡((d+m2)εs​c​o​r​e)K=\frac{d}{\sigma^{2}_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}}\log\left(\frac{(d+m_{2})}{\varepsilon_{score}}\right), then:

KL(ptδ∥p^tδ)≤(d+m2)e−T+e4h′k2εs​c​o​r​e2∑k=1K14​(tk−t′k)\displaystyle KL(p_{t_{\delta}}\|\hat{p}_{t_{\delta}})\leq(d+m_{2})e^{-T}+e^{4}{h^{\prime}}_{k}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}_{score}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{4{(t_{k}-{t^{\prime}}_{k})}} (10)

where t0′=δ>0t^{\prime}_{0}=\delta>0

Proof.

The proof can be found in the Appendix B. Again similar to the idea of Theorem 3.1 proof, we have to consider both initialization error and the error due to empirical ODE (eq. 6). However, since the score function hasn’t been provided as smooth here, bounding the error due to the empirical ODE will be a bit more tricky here. Taking inspiration from the previous works, we first try to bound the operator norm of the score function along the true trajectory since, using the fact that the forward process is just a convolution with gaussian distribution and the perturbation can be bounded. ∎

It is easy to observe that absence of smoothness (the constant LL) induces a factor of dd but the remaining result is similar to the previous theorem and thus, we can again have a similar conclusion as follows.

Corollary 3.4.

Under Assumptions 3.1, 3.2, Algorithm 1 achieves the KL divergence error O⁡(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2}), if we run it for a total time T=log⁡(d+m2ϵ)T=\log(\frac{d+m_{2}}{\epsilon}) with the constant step size, say, hk=1−e−δ2​dh_{k}=\frac{1-e^{-\delta}}{2d} and hk′=1−e−δdh^{\prime}_{k}=\frac{1-e^{-\delta}}{d}, thereby inducing an iteration/discretization complexity K=Thk=2​d1−e−δ​log⁡(d+m2ϵ)K=\frac{T}{h_{k}}=\frac{2d}{1-e^{-\delta}}\log(\frac{d+m_{2}}{\epsilon}) given that the score estimation error from denoising score matching is εs​c​o​r​e=O⁡(ϵlog⁡(d+m2ϵ))\varepsilon_{score}=O\left(\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{\log(\frac{d+m_{2}}{\epsilon})}}\right), better then any of the existing results [2] (O⁡(dϵ2))\left(O\left(\frac{d}{\epsilon^{2}}\right)\right) for DDPM [15] sampler when the smoothness of the score function is not assumed.

Both this theorem and the previous theorem 3.1 suffer from the limitation of hk′h^{\prime}_{k} being bounded. This limits their applicability to the original consistency model formulation [31] which always takes as the end of the reverse flow ODE (or the data distribution)and thus for that the sequence tk′t^{\prime}_{k} should be set to 0. This issue has further been discussed in the appendix after the proof of Lemma A.4.
Seeing the proof of both these theorems, it can be observed that the analysis is almost tight and thus, to resolve this limitation, exploring other metrics like TV distance might be an interesting direction. We now discuss learning the consistency function formulation f^\hat{f} corresponding to the empirical ODE using the distillation technique proposed in the consistency model paper [31].

3.5 Consistency Distillation Training to estimate f^\hat{f}

In the previous subsection, we discussed how we can exploit the given formulation of the consistency function i.e. f^​(t′,t,𝐱t)\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,{\mathbf{x}}_{t}) corresponding to the empirical PF ODE to achieve state of the art convergence results when doing iterative multi-step sampling. However, it is still not clear whether such a consistency function correponding to empirical ODE (eq. 6) can be learned efficiently or not. In this section, we discuss this learning of such consistency function.

The original consistency model paper proposes two schemes to learn any consistency function: distillation based training and the self-consistency training. Here, we will consider the first case. It involves using an ODE solver Φ\Phi and distilling its knowledge into the consistency model. Let us denote the parameterized approximation of f^\hat{f} as f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta}. The distillation based training involves considering the true process at tk+1t_{k+1}: 𝐱tk+1=e−tk+1​𝐱0+1−e−2​tk+1​ϵ,{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{k+1}}=e^{-t_{k+1}}{\mathbf{x}}_{0}+\sqrt{1-e^{-2t_{k+1}}}\epsilon, ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and taking one step back to get 𝒙^tkϕ\hat{{\bm{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{k}} using a pretrained diffusion model as ODE solver ϕ\phi and the empirical PF ODE, denoting this overall one step update as Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot) :

𝒙^tkϕ=Φ⁡(𝐱tk+1,tk+1,tk)=𝐱tk+1−(tk+1−tk)​s^tk+1​(𝐱tk+1)\displaystyle\hat{{\bm{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{k}}=\Phi({\mathbf{x}}_{t_{k+1}},t_{k+1},t_{k})={\mathbf{x}}_{t_{k+1}}-({t_{k+1}-t_{k}})\hat{s}_{t_{k+1}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t_{k+1}}) (11)

The objective ℒC​D\mathcal{L}_{CD} then is to feed both of these to f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta} and minimize the euclidean distance between the resulting outputs:

ℒCD​(θ,θ−,Φ):=𝔼⁡[λ⁡(tn)​‖f^θ​(0,tn+1,𝐱tn+1)−f^θ−​(0,tn,𝒙^tnΦ)‖22]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{CD}}(\theta,\theta^{-};\Phi):=\mathbb{E}\left[\lambda(t_{n})\left\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(0,t_{n+1},{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{n+1}})-\hat{f}_{\theta^{-}}(0,t_{n},\hat{{\bm{x}}}^{\Phi}_{t_{n}})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right] (12)

where θ−\theta^{-}is just the running averages of the parameters, done for a stable training and also for faster convergence and λ⁡(⋅)∈ℝ+\lambda(\cdot)\in\mathbb{R}^{+} is just a positive weighing function [31]. Now, to analyze the difference between true consistency function and the learned consistency function f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta} via the above objective, we first state some assumptions on the training as well as on the parametrized function f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta} itself. These are again standard in literature and have been used the all recent works invovlving consistency model analysis [18, 31, 26].

Assumption 3.4.

We have the following assumption [31, 26] on consistency distillation error for the approximator of f^\hat{f} i.e. f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta}:

𝔼𝐱tk+1∼ptk+1​[‖f^θ​(tk−1′,tk+1,𝐱tk+1)−f^θ​(tk−1′,tk,𝒙^tkϕ)‖22]≤εcd2​(tk+1−tk)2,∀k∈[1,K−1],\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{k+1}}\sim p_{t_{k+1}}}\left[\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{k-1},t_{k+1},{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{k+1}})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{k-1},t_{k},\hat{{\bm{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{k}})\|_{2}^{2}\right]\leq\varepsilon^{2}_{\text{cd}}(t_{k+1}-t_{k})^{2},\quad\forall\,k\in[1,K-1], (13)
Assumption 3.5.

f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta} is Lf−L_{f}-lipschitz [18, 31, 26].

Verifying Assumption 3.5. Since we have assumed that 𝒔^t\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t} is smooth in one of the analysis above, it is straightforward to verify that f^(t′,t,⋅)\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,\cdot) would satisfy the following approximately:

f^​(t′,t,x)≈(1+(t−t′))​x+(t−t′)​𝒔t​(x).\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,x)\approx(1+(t-t^{\prime}))x+(t-t^{\prime}){\bm{s}}_{t}(x).

Therefore, we will have:

‖f^​(t′,t,x)−f^​(t′,t,y)‖2\displaystyle\|\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,x)-\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,y)\|_{2} ≈‖(1+(t−t′))​(x−y)+(t−t′)​(𝒔^t​(x)−𝒔^t​(y))‖2\displaystyle\approx\|\left(1+(t-t^{\prime})\right)(x-y)+(t-t^{\prime})(\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(x)-\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(y))\|_{2}
≤(1+(t−t′))​‖(x−y)‖2+(t−t′)​‖(𝒔^t​(x)−𝒔^t​(y))‖2\displaystyle\leq\left(1+(t-t^{\prime})\right)\|(x-y)\|_{2}+(t-t^{\prime})\|(\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(x)-\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(y))\|_{2}
≤(1+(1+L)​(t−t′))​‖x−y‖2\displaystyle\leq\left(1+(1+L)(t-t^{\prime})\right)\|x-y\|_{2}

where LL is the Lipschitz of 𝒔^t\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t} (Assumption 3.3). For the case when t−t′t-t^{\prime} is small a tight upper bound is:

‖f^​(t′,t,x)−f^​(t′,t,y)‖≤e(1+L)​(t−t′)​‖x−y‖\|\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,x)-\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,y)\|\leq e^{(1+L)(t-t^{\prime})}\|x-y\|

Thus, assuming that f^\hat{f} would be lipschitz smooth is a reasonable assumption and LfL_{f} would be approximately same as (1+(1+L)​(t−t′))(1+(1+L)(t-t^{\prime})). Also, we can now directly extend this finding to f^θ​(t′,t,x)\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime},t,x) since it should just incur some additional error related to εc​d\varepsilon_{cd} which would be of other order O⁡((t−t′)​εc​d)O((t-t^{\prime})\varepsilon_{cd}). This will lead to the following:

‖f^θ​(tn−1′,tn,𝒙tn)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tn,𝒚tn)‖2≲(tn−tn−1′)​(εcd)+Lf​‖𝒙tn−𝒚tn‖2.\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n},{\bm{x}}_{t_{n}})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n},{\bm{y}}_{t_{n}})\|_{2}\lesssim(t_{n}-t^{\prime}_{n-1})(\varepsilon_{\text{cd}})+L_{f}\|{\bm{x}}_{t_{n}}-{\bm{y}}_{t_{n}}\|_{2}.

Therefore, we can assume that f^θ(t′,t,⋅)\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime},t,\cdot) would be LfL_{f}-lipschitz.

We now provide the following theorem regarding the difference between the estimated consistency function using the distillation based training and true consistency function corresponding to the PF-ODE using the above assumptions.

Theorem 3.5.

(Bounding error between f^\hat{f} and estimated f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta}). Following the definition of f^\hat{f} for some discretization {tn}n∈[1,N]\{t_{n}\}_{n\in[1,N]} for the consistency distillation training, under assumption 3.1-3.5, we have:

𝔼​‖f^θ​(tn−1′,tn,𝐱n)−f^​(tn−1′,tn,𝐱n)‖22≤Lf​ehn−1/2​(L3/2​d1/2​hn−1)+εc​d​(tn−t1)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n},{\mathbf{x}}_{n})-\hat{f}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n},{\mathbf{x}}_{n})\|^{2}_{2}\leq L_{f}e^{{h_{n-1}}/{2}}(L^{{3}/{2}}d^{{1}/{2}}h_{n-1})+\varepsilon_{cd}(t_{n}-t_{1})

.

Proof.

For proof, please refer Appendix C. ∎

Achieving a good approximation of f^\hat{f}. Based, on the previous theorem, it is easy to observe that the approximation mainly depends on the consistency distillation training error and the training time discretization, both of which can be made arbitrarily small during training and thus, we can argue achieving a very close approximation for f^\hat{f}. Now, we will again consider this approximation analysis but this time when the smoothness assumption on score function is not provided.

Non-smooth case.

We will now consider the scenario where we do not have assumption 3.5 where we have shown how to bound the expected value for ‖∇𝒔t​(⋅)‖\|\nabla{\bm{s}}_{t}(\cdot)\| on the true trajectory, since if 𝒔^t\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t} is not smooth, we cannot verify it and thus, is not a good assumption to have. Here, will use the idea from the proof of theorem 3.3 and will bound the expected difference instead. We can understand this for the true ff first as follows for some 𝐱,𝐲∈ℝd{\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:

𝔼​‖f^​(t′,t,𝐱)−f^​(t′,t,𝐲)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,{\mathbf{x}})-\hat{f}(t^{\prime},t,{\mathbf{y}})\|_{2}
≈𝔼​‖(1+(t−t′))​(𝐱−𝐲)+(t−t′)​(𝒔t​(𝐱)−𝒔t​(𝐲))‖2\displaystyle\approx\mathbb{E}\|(1+(t-t^{\prime}))({\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}})+(t-t^{\prime})({\bm{s}}_{t}({\mathbf{x}})-{\bm{s}}_{t}({\mathbf{y}}))\|_{2}
≤(t−t′)E∥𝐱−𝐲∥2+dσt2(t−t′)E[∥𝐱−𝐲∥2exp(‖𝐱−𝐲‖σt2),](lemma B.2)\displaystyle\leq(t-t^{\prime})E\|{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}\|_{2}+\frac{d}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}(t-t^{\prime})E\left[\|{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}\|_{2}\exp\left(\frac{\|{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}\|}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}\right),\right]\qquad\text{(lemma \ref{expected_smooth})}
≤(t−t′)E∥𝐱−𝐲∥2+C6​dσt2(t−t′)E∥𝐱−𝐲∥2(when 𝐱,𝐲 are close)\displaystyle\leq(t-t^{\prime})E\|{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}\|_{2}+\frac{C_{6}d}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}(t-t^{\prime})E\|{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}\|_{2}\qquad\text{(when ${\mathbf{x}},{\mathbf{y}}$ are close)}

Now, we provide the following lemma as a counterpart of lemma 3.5 for f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta} in this case:

Lemma 3.6.

(Validation the assumption on f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta} in the non-smooth case.) Using the exponential integrator while the consistency distillation training:

𝒙^tnϕ=etn+1−tn​𝐱tn+1+(etn+1−tn−1)​𝒔^tn+1​(𝐱tn+1),\hat{{\bm{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n}}=e^{t_{n+1}-t_{n}}{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{n+1}}+(e^{t_{n+1}-t_{n}}-1)\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t_{n+1}}({\mathbf{x}}_{t_{n+1}}),

and given the assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, we have:

𝔼​‖fθ​(t1,tn,𝐱tn)−fθ​(t1,tn,𝐲tn)‖2\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|f_{\theta}(t_{1},t_{n},{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{n}})-f_{\theta}(t_{1},t_{n},{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{n}})\|_{2} ≤2​(tn−t1)​εc​d+2​εs​c​o​r​e​(tn−t1)+n​𝔼​‖𝐱tn−𝐲tn‖2\displaystyle\leq 2(t_{n}-t_{1})\varepsilon_{cd}+2\varepsilon_{score}(t_{n}-t_{1})+n\mathbb{E}\|{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{n}}-{\mathbf{y}}_{t_{n}}\|_{2}

where again 𝐲tn{\bm{y}}_{t_{n}} lie on a (correspond to) different probability flow ODEs (for a given time-stamp tnt_{n}).

Proof.

A rough sketch would be similar to the proof of lemma provided in [26]. However, since we donot assume smoothness, we will instead work with the expectation and use our lemma B.2 for bounding it by bounding the expected hessian (or gradient of score). Please refer Appendix C for the complete proof. It is straightforward to further adapt for any tn−1′t^{\prime}_{n-1} as the first parameter as against t1t_{1}. It has been omitted here for simplicity. ∎

Now, we again provide the analysis for the approximated consistency model (counterpart of Theorem 3.5) for the non-smooth case:

Theorem 3.7.

Following the definition of f^\hat{f} for some discretization {tn}n∈[1,N]\{t_{n}\}_{n\in[1,N]} in the consistency distillation training, using assumptions 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, we have:

𝔼​‖f⁡(tn−1′,tn,𝐱n)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tn,𝐱n)‖2≤n​ehn−1/2​(L3/2​d1/2​hn−1)+(tn−t1)​(3​εc​d+2​εs​c​o​r​e)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\|f(t_{n-1}^{\prime},t_{n},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t_{n-1}^{\prime},t_{n},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n})\|_{2}\leq ne^{{h_{n-1}}/{2}}(L^{{3}/{2}}d^{{1}/{2}}h_{n-1})+(t_{n}-t_{1})\left(3\varepsilon_{cd}+2\varepsilon_{score}\right)
Proof.

The proof is similar as Theorem 3.5 but here we instead utilize the Lemma 3.6 and bound the expectation of the term. It incurs a factor of dd which arises from the bound on the hessian. Also, here as against Theorem 3.5, we have bounded the error w.r.t. the true consistency function corresponding to the actual reverse ODE and thus, we incur the additional term involving the score estimation. The detailed proof is provided in Appendix C. ∎

4 Conclusions

In this work, we provided a theoritical analysis for multi-step generation using consistency models, showing that the number of iterations KK (and consequently the step size) for the probability flow ODE based generation can be independent of ϵ\epsilon to generate samples from a distribution which is ϵ2−\epsilon^{2}-close in KL divergence to the target distribution, under minimal assumptions. Here, we have achieved O⁡(d​log⁡(dϵ))O(d\log(\frac{d}{\epsilon})) convergence which is both state-of-the-art w.r.t. to dimension dd and also w.r.t. ϵ\epsilon since it has a logarithmic dependence as agaisnt O⁡(1ϵ)O(\frac{1}{\epsilon}) in the current best ODE/SDE based samplers. We also don’t require any strict assumptions on Divergence/Jacobi in our ODE based generation as the existing works utilizing the deterministic probability flow ODEs for generation and even relax the smoothness assumption. Furthermore, we also provide a theoretical analysis for estimating the formulation of the consistency function required for our analysis: which can take a point at a given time instant to arbitrary time instants along the reverse probability flow ODE. We show that this can be efficiently estimated using the distillation objective proposed in the original consistency models paper, given we use a fine discretization at the training time. It can be concluded from this article that since we can learn consistency functions efficiently and the multistep sampling algorithms using them are much faster theoretically than the DDPM type samples, these consistency models can emerge as a powerful alternative and can be quite useful in large-scale real-world setups.

Appendix A Proof of Theorem 3.1

Here, we provide the proof of our first main result. As highlighted in the high level proof in the main paper, we bound the two errors: the error due to empirical PF ODE and the initialization error. We first discuss bounding the former below.

Error due to the empirical PF ODE (eq. 6).

As discussed in the algorithms provided in the main, we will denote the joint distribution of the true and approximate process by pt1,t2,…,tKp_{t_{1},t_{2},...,t_{K}} and p^t1,t2,…,tK\hat{p}_{t_{1},t_{2},...,t_{K}} respectively. The overall idea is to bound the KL between the outputs using the data processing inequality and bounding the KL between p^t1,t2,…,tK\hat{p}_{t_{1},t_{2},...,t_{K}} and pt1,t2,…,tKp_{t_{1},t_{2},...,t_{K}} which can be done by rewriting them using transition (conditional) probabilities. The following two lemmas describe this idea.
Notational Remark. As discussed in the Subsection 3.1 of the main paper, we will use the notations 𝐱tk{\mathbf{x}}_{t_{k}} and 𝐱k{\mathbf{x}}_{k} interchangeably both corresponding to true (resp. empirical) PF ODE at time tkt_{k} (resp. tk−1′t^{\prime}_{k-1}) for a given sequence {tk}\{t_{k}\} (resp. {tk′}\{t^{\prime}_{k}\}).

Lemma A.1.

Denoting p^k−1|k\hat{p}_{k-1|k} be the conditional probability of 𝐱^k−1\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k-1} given 𝐱^k\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k}, and let pk−1|k{p}_{k-1|k} be the conditional probability of 𝐱k−1{\mathbf{x}}_{k-1} given 𝐱k{\mathbf{x}}_{k}. Then

KL(pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k)∥p^k−1|k(⋅|𝐱k))=e2​(tk−1′−tk−1)‖f⁡(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k)−f^​(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k)‖222​(1−e2​(tk−1′−tk−1))\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\big\|\hat{p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\right)=e^{2(t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1})}\frac{\|f(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})-\hat{f}(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}}{2(1-e^{2(t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1})})}
Proof.

For this, we know that from Algorithm 2 that the conditional pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k){p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k}) is the following Gaussain:

pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k)∼𝒩(etk−1′−tk−1f(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k),(1−e2​(tk−1′−tk−1))Id){p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\sim\mathcal{N}\left(e^{t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1}}f(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{\mathbf{x}}_{k}),\left(1-e^{2(t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1})}\right)I_{d}\right)

where IdI_{d} is the d-dimensional identity matrix. Similarly, from Algorithm 1:

p^k−1|k(⋅|𝐱k)∼𝒩(etk−1′−tk−1f^(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k),(1−e2​(tk−1′−tk−1))Id)\hat{p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\sim\mathcal{N}\left(e^{t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1}}\hat{f}(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{\mathbf{x}}_{k}),\left(1-e^{2(t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1})}\right)I_{d}\right)

Now, since the covariance matrices are same for both, we can just use the following formulae for calculating KL between two gaussians with different means but same variance:

KL(pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k)∥pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k))=12(μ1−μ2)T∑(μ1−μ2)\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\big\|{p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\right)=\frac{1}{2}(\mu_{1}-\mu_{2})^{T}\sum(\mu_{1}-\mu_{2})

where μ1\mu_{1}, μ2\mu_{2} corresponds to the mean of the two distributions and ∑\sum corresponds to their covariance. For this case, we have:

μ1\displaystyle\mu_{1} =etk−1′−tk−1​f​(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k)\displaystyle=e^{t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1}}f(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{\mathbf{x}}_{k})
μ2\displaystyle\mu_{2} =etk−1′−tk−1​f^​(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k)\displaystyle=e^{t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1}}\hat{f}(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{\mathbf{x}}_{k})
Σ\displaystyle\Sigma =(1−e2​(tk−1′−tk−1))​Id\displaystyle=\left(1-e^{2(t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1})}\right)I_{d}

Merely substituting these values in the KL formulae will lead to the desired term.
∎

We will now utilize this expression to bound the KL between outputs of Algorithms 1 and 2 using the following lemma:

Lemma A.2.

We have

KL(pt0∥p^t0)≤\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{t_{0}}\big\|\hat{p}_{t_{0}}\right)\leq KL(pt1,t2,…,tK∥p^t1,t2,…,tK)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{t_{1},t_{2},...,t_{K}}\big\|\hat{p}_{t_{1},t_{2},...,t_{K}}\right)
=\displaystyle= KL(ptK∥p^tK)+𝔼pt1,..,tK[∑k=1KKL(pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k)∥p^k−1|k(⋅|𝐱k))]\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{t_{K}}\big\|\hat{p}_{t_{K}}\right)+\mathbb{E}_{{p}_{t_{1},..,t_{K}}}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\big\|\hat{p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\right)\right]
Proof.

Since we know that LHS corresponds to first marginalizing the corresponding joint distributions and then calculating KL and RHS is the KL div between the joint distributions. Using data processing inequality, it is straightforward to argue that the inequality holds. The second equation is just decomposing the KL of the joint distribution into conditionals which can be easily verified by merely writing the RHS expression using the KL formulae. ∎

We now provide another lemma which will be useful in relating the expected difference between the true and approximate process generated from empirical PF ODE with the corresponding consistency functions.

Lemma A.3.

Given deterministic functions gg and g^\hat{g} on a random variable 𝐲{\mathbf{y}} and also given random variables 𝐱,𝐱^{\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}} such that 𝐱=g⁡(𝐲){\mathbf{x}}=g({\mathbf{y}}) and 𝐱^=g^​(𝐲)\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}=\hat{g}({\mathbf{y}}), then we have:

𝔼𝐱,𝐱^​‖𝐱−𝐱^‖2=𝔼𝐲​‖g⁡(𝐲)−g^​(𝐲)‖2\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}}\|{\mathbf{x}}-\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}\|^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{y}}}\|g({\mathbf{y}})-\hat{g}({\mathbf{y}})\|^{2}
Proof.

We can write expectation of a deterministic function of random variables:

𝔼𝐱,𝐱^[h(𝐱,𝐱^]=∫∫h(𝐱,𝐱^)f𝐱,𝐱^(𝒙,𝒙^)d𝒙d𝒙^\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}}[h({\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}]=\int\int h({\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}})f_{{\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}}({\bm{x}},\hat{{\bm{x}}})d{\bm{x}}d\hat{{\bm{x}}}

where f𝐱,𝐱^f_{{\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}} is the joint distribution of the two random variables. Now, since we know that 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}, 𝐱^\hat{{\mathbf{x}}} are not independent and each correspond to a deterministic function of some random variable 𝐲{\mathbf{y}} where 𝐱=g⁡(𝐲){\mathbf{x}}=g({\mathbf{y}}) and 𝐱^=g^​(𝐲)\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}=\hat{g}({\mathbf{y}}). Thus, if we know 𝐲{\mathbf{y}}, we have the value of 𝐱{\mathbf{x}}, 𝐱^\hat{{\mathbf{x}}} fixed and thus, we can use the change of variables in the previous expression:

𝔼𝐱,𝐱^​[h⁡(𝒙,𝒙^)]=∫∫⁡h⁡(𝒙,𝒙^)​f𝐱,𝐱^​(𝒙,𝒙^)​𝑑𝒙​𝑑𝒙^=∫h⁡(g⁡(𝒚),g^​(𝒚))​f𝐲​(𝒚)​𝑑𝒚=𝔼𝐲​[h⁡(g⁡(𝒚),g^​(𝒚))]\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}}[h({\bm{x}},\hat{{\bm{x}}})]=\int\int h({\bm{x}},\hat{{\bm{x}}})f_{{\mathbf{x}},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}}({\bm{x}},\hat{{\bm{x}}})d{\bm{x}}d\hat{{\bm{x}}}=\int h(g({\bm{y}}),\hat{g}({\bm{y}}))f_{\mathbf{y}}({\bm{y}})d{\bm{y}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{y}}[h(g({\bm{y}}),\hat{g}({\bm{y}}))]

where f𝐲f_{\mathbf{y}} is the distribution of 𝐲{\mathbf{y}} given hh is measurable. Now, using the choice of hh as ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|^{2}, which satisfies the requirement, leads to our result. ∎

≤exp((2+2L+1hk′)hk′)(∫tk−1′tkhk′εs​c​o​r​e2dt)(using Assumption 3.1)\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(\left(2+2L+\frac{1}{h^{\prime}_{k}}\right)h^{\prime}_{k}\right)\left(\int_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}^{t_{k}}h^{\prime}_{k}\,\varepsilon^{2}_{score}dt\right)\quad\text{(using Assumption \ref{assumption_score_est})}

𝔼pt1,..,tK​‖f⁡(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k)−f^​(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k)‖22<e2​(h′k2​εs​c​o​r​e2)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{p}_{t_{1},..,t_{K}}}\|f(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})-\hat{f}(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}<e^{2}({h^{\prime}}_{k}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}_{score}) (14)

Setting {tk′}=0\{t^{\prime}_{k}\}=0 to replicate the original consistency models? A possibility of setting the sequence tk′=0t^{\prime}_{k}=0 is there but then hk′<12​(1+L)h^{\prime}_{k}<\frac{1}{2(1+L)} is not guaranteed and for this, we can just instead use hk′=O⁡(log⁡(1/δ))h^{\prime}_{k}={O}(\log(1/\delta)) but then εs​c​o​r​e=O⁡(δL+1.5l​o​g​(1/δ))\varepsilon_{score}={O}(\frac{\delta^{L+1.5}}{\sqrt{log(1/\delta)}}), where L≥1L\geq 1, which would thus require a very accurate estimation of score as against O~​(L​δ)\tilde{O}(L\delta) before. Thus, as highlighted in the main paper its adaptation to the original consistency model formulation is not straightforward.

Initialization Error.

If we define the forward noising process for a total time TT (and consequently KK total iterations where ∑k=0Khk+t0=T\sum_{k=0}^{K}h_{k}+t_{0}=T), we know that the pT=l​a​w​(𝐱T)p_{T}={law}({\mathbf{x}}_{T}) is still not exactly 𝒩⁡(0,Id)\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and is just close to it. So when we initialize the reverse/generation process with gaussian, this leads to the initialization error which is the difference between the distribution after running the forward process on the original data distribution for time TT and the standard gaussian distribution, which can be bounded as follows:

Lemma A.5.

(Convergence of the OU process). Under Assumption 3.2, for T>1T>1, we have

KL(pT∥γd)≤(d+m2)e−T.KL(p_{T}\parallel\gamma_{d})\leq(d+m_{2})e^{-T}.

where TT is the total time for the forward process and m2=𝔼pt​[‖𝐱‖22]m_{2}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}[\|{\bm{x}}\|_{2}^{2}].

Proof.

For any t>0t>0, we can use Jensen’s inequality to bound the entropy of ptp_{t}:

∫ℝdpt​(𝒙)​log⁡pt​(𝒙)​𝑑𝒙\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p_{t}({\bm{x}})\log p_{t}({\bm{x}})\,d{\bm{x}} =∫ℝd(∫ℝdpt|0​(𝒙|𝒙0)​𝑑P​(𝒙0))​log⁡(∫ℝdpt|0​(𝒙|𝒙0)​𝑑P​(𝒙0))​𝑑𝒙\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p_{t|0}({\bm{x}}|{\bm{x}}_{0})dP({\bm{x}}_{0})\right)\log\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p_{t|0}({\bm{x}}|{\bm{x}}_{0})dP({\bm{x}}_{0})\right)d{\bm{x}}
≤∫ℝd(∫ℝdpt|0​(𝒙|𝒙0)​log⁡pt|0​(𝒙|𝒙0)​𝑑P​(𝒙0))​𝑑𝒙\displaystyle\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p_{t|0}({\bm{x}}|{\bm{x}}_{0})\log p_{t|0}({\bm{x}}|{\bm{x}}_{0})dP({\bm{x}}_{0})\right)d{\bm{x}}
=∫ℝd(∫ℝdpt|0​(𝒙|𝒙0)​log⁡pt|0​(𝒙|𝒙0)​𝑑𝒙)​𝑑P​(𝒙0).\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p_{t|0}({\bm{x}}|{\bm{x}}_{0})\log p_{t|0}({\bm{x}}|{\bm{x}}_{0})d{\bm{x}}\right)dP({\bm{x}}_{0}).

Since for the considered OU proces, we have 𝐱t|𝐱0∼𝒩⁡(αt​x0,σt2​Id){\mathbf{x}}_{t}|{\mathbf{x}}_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(\alpha_{t}x_{0},\sigma_{t}^{2}I_{d}), where σt2=1−e−t\sigma_{t}^{2}=1-e^{-t}, we have

∫ℝdpt|0​(𝒙|𝒙0)​log⁡pt|0​(𝒙|𝒙0)​𝑑𝒙=−d2​log⁡(2​π​σt2)−d2.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p_{t|0}({\bm{x}}|{\bm{x}}_{0})\log p_{t|0}({\bm{x}}|{\bm{x}}_{0})\,d{\bm{x}}=-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma_{t}^{2})-\frac{d}{2}.

Thus,

∫ℝdpt​(𝒙)​log⁡pt​(𝒙)​𝑑𝒙≤−d2​log⁡(2​π​σt2)−d2.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p_{t}({\bm{x}})\log p_{t}({\bm{x}})\,d{\bm{x}}\leq-\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma_{t}^{2})-\frac{d}{2}.

Therefore,

KL(pt∥γd)=∫ℝdpt(𝒙)logpt(𝒙)d𝒙+𝔼pt[∥𝒙∥22+d2log(2π)]≤d2logσt−2+12(m2−d).KL(p_{t}\parallel\gamma_{d})=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}p_{t}({\bm{x}})\log p_{t}({\bm{x}})\,d{\bm{x}}+\mathbb{E}_{p_{t}}\left[\|{\bm{x}}\|^{2}_{2}+\frac{d}{2}\log(2\pi)\right]\leq\frac{d}{2}\log\sigma_{t}^{-2}+\frac{1}{2}(m_{2}-d).

From the exponential convergence of Langevin dynamics with a strongly log-concave stationary distribution, we obtain

KL(pT∥γd)≤e−T+t(d2logσt−2+12(m2−d)).KL(p_{T}\parallel\gamma_{d})\leq e^{-T+t}\left(\frac{d}{2}\log\sigma_{t}^{-2}+\frac{1}{2}(m_{2}-d)\right).

By choosing t=log⁡2t=\log 2, we have

et​log⁡(1σt2)≤1.e^{t}\log\left(\frac{1}{\sigma_{t}^{2}}\right)\leq 1.

Thus,

KL(pT∥γd)≤e−T(d+m2).KL(p_{T}\parallel\gamma_{d})\leq e^{-T}(d+m_{2}).

∎

Proving Theorem 3.1.

Given the above lemmas corresponding to the error components, we now provide the proof for Theorem 3.3 as follows:

Proof.

From Lemma A.2, we have:

KL(pt0∥p^t0)≤\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{t_{0}}\big\|\hat{p}_{t_{0}}\right)\leq KL(pt1,t2,…,tK∥p^t1,t2,…,tK)\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{t_{1},t_{2},...,t_{K}}\big\|\hat{p}_{t_{1},t_{2},...,t_{K}}\right)
=\displaystyle= KL(ptK∥p^tK)+𝔼pt1,..,tK[∑k=1KKL(pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k)∥p^k−1|k(⋅|𝐱k))]\displaystyle\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{t_{K}}\big\|\hat{p}_{t_{K}}\right)+\mathbb{E}_{{p}_{t_{1},..,t_{K}}}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\big\|\hat{p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\right)\right]

From Lemma A.1, the conditional KL divergence between pk−1|k{p}_{k-1|k} and p^k−1|k\hat{p}_{k-1|k} is given by:

KL(pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k)∥p^k−1|k(⋅|𝐱k))=e2​(tk−1′−tk−1)‖f⁡(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k)−f^​(tk−1′,tk,𝐱k)‖222​(1−e2​(tk−1′−tk−1))\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\big\|\hat{p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\right)=e^{2(t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1})}\frac{\|f(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})-\hat{f}(t_{k-1}^{\prime},t_{k},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}}{2(1-e^{2(t_{k-1}^{\prime}-t_{k-1})})}

Substituting this into the sum in Lemma A.2, we get:

Appendix B Proof of theorem 3.3

The proof in this part also similar to the proof in the previous section, however, since we do not have an assumption on the smoothness of the score function, we need to find an alternate way to control the ‖𝒔t​(𝐱t)−𝒔t​(𝐱^t)‖2\|{\bm{s}}_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{t})-{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})\|^{2} term in Lemma A.4. For this, we take inspiration from literature [3, 1] on SDE based diffusion analysis which analyses in the absence of smoothness assumptions. We begin by first providing a lemma adapted from [3] that bounds the Gaussian perturbation of a given probability distribution in d−d-dimension as follows.

Lemma B.1.

(Taken from [3]). Let PP be a probability measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Consider the density of its Gaussian perturbation

pσ​(𝒙)∝∫ℝdexp⁡(−‖𝒙−𝒚‖22​σ2)​𝑑P​(𝒚).p_{\sigma}({\bm{x}})\propto\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\exp\left(-\frac{\|{\bm{x}}-{\bm{y}}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)dP({\bm{y}}).

Then for 𝐱∼pσ{\mathbf{x}}\sim p_{\sigma}, we have the sub-exponential norm bound

‖∇2​log​pσ​(𝐱)‖F,ψ1≲dσ2,\|\nabla^{2}\log p_{\sigma}({\mathbf{x}})\|_{F,\psi_{1}}\lesssim\frac{d}{\sigma^{2}},

where ∥⋅∥F,ψ1=∥∥⋅∥F∥ψ1\|\cdot\|_{F,\psi_{1}}=\|\|\cdot\|_{F}\|_{\psi_{1}} denotes the sub-exponential norm of the Frobenius norm of a random matrix.

Proof.

We just provide a sketch here for reference. For the detailed proof please refer Lemma 12 in [3]. First, we will have the following equation for conditional density P~σ​(𝒚|𝒙)\tilde{P}_{\sigma}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}}):

d​P~σ​(𝒚|𝒙)∝exp⁡(−‖𝒚−𝒙‖22​σ2)​d​P​(𝒚).d\tilde{P}_{\sigma}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})\propto\exp\left(-\frac{\|{\bm{y}}-{\bm{x}}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)dP({\bm{y}}).

Now, just writing ∇2​log​pσ\nabla^{2}\log p_{\sigma} in terms of VarP~σ​(𝒚|𝒙)⁡(𝒚σ2)\operatorname{Var}_{\tilde{P}_{\sigma}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})}\left(\frac{{\bm{y}}}{\sigma^{2}}\right) and using the following inequality for any integer qq:

𝔼pσ​(𝒙)​[‖VarP~σ​(𝒚|𝒙)⁡(𝒚/σ2)‖Fq]≤1σ2​p​𝔼pσ​(x)​[𝔼P~σ​(𝒚|𝒙)​‖(𝒚−𝒙)/σ⁡(𝒚−𝒙)/σ⊤‖Fq].\mathbb{E}_{p_{\sigma}({\bm{x}})}\left[\|\operatorname{Var}_{\tilde{P}_{\sigma}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})}({\bm{y}}/\sigma^{2})\|_{F}^{q}\right]\leq\frac{1}{\sigma^{2p}}\mathbb{E}_{p_{\sigma}(x)}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{P}_{\sigma}({\bm{y}}|{\bm{x}})}\|({\bm{y}}-{\bm{x}})/\sigma({\bm{y}}-{\bm{x}})/\sigma^{\top}\|_{F}^{q}\right].

and using the fact that 𝐲−𝐱σ\frac{{\mathbf{y}}-{\mathbf{x}}}{\sigma} is normally distributed, we can derive the result.

∎

We have:

Lemma B.3.

For any δ>0\delta>0 with εs​c​o​r​e=O⁡(δ)\varepsilon_{score}=O(\delta), we can choose tk−1′t^{\prime}_{k-1} such that hk′=tk−tk−1′<1d2h^{\prime}_{k}=t_{k}-t^{\prime}_{k-1}<\frac{1}{d^{2}}, and consequently discretization hk=tk−tk−1<1d2h_{k}=t_{k}-t_{k-1}<\frac{1}{d^{2}} (since tk−1′<tk−1t^{\prime}_{k-1}<t_{k-1} thus hkh_{k}<hk′h^{\prime}_{k}) and have:

≤2​𝔼​‖Δt‖2+2​𝔼​[‖Δt‖​(‖𝒔t​(𝐱t)−𝒔t​(𝐱^t)‖+‖𝒔t​(𝐱^t)−𝒔^t​(𝐱^t)‖)]\displaystyle\leq 2\mathbb{E}\|\Delta_{t}\|^{2}+2\mathbb{E}\left[\|\Delta_{t}\|\left(\|{\bm{s}}_{t}({\mathbf{x}}_{t})-{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})\|+\|{\bm{s}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})-\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})\|\right)\right]

≤(2+1hk′+1hk′)𝔼∥Δt∥2+h′kε2s​c​o​r​e+d2​hk′σt4𝔼[∥Δt∥2exp(‖Δt‖22​σt2)](Assumption 3.1)\displaystyle\leq\left(2+\frac{1}{h^{\prime}_{k}}+\frac{1}{h^{\prime}_{k}}\right)\mathbb{E}\|\Delta_{t}\|^{2}+h^{\prime}_{k}\varepsilon^{2}_{score}+\frac{d^{2}h^{\prime}_{k}}{\sigma_{t}^{4}}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\Delta_{t}\|^{2}\exp\left(\frac{\|\Delta_{t}\|^{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}\right)\right]\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{(Assumption \ref{assumption_score_est})}
=(2+1hk′+1hk′)​𝔼​‖Δt‖2+hk′​εs​c​o​r​e2+d2​hk′σt4​𝔼​[‖Δt‖2]+d2​hk′σt4​𝔼​[‖Δt‖2​(exp⁡(‖Δt‖22​σt2)−1)]\displaystyle=\left(2+\frac{1}{h^{\prime}_{k}}+\frac{1}{h^{\prime}_{k}}\right)\mathbb{E}\|\Delta_{t}\|^{2}+h^{\prime}_{k}\varepsilon^{2}_{score}+\frac{d^{2}h^{\prime}_{k}}{\sigma_{t}^{4}}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\Delta_{t}\|^{2}\right]+\frac{d^{2}h^{\prime}_{k}}{\sigma_{t}^{4}}\mathbb{E}\left[\|\Delta_{t}\|^{2}\left(\exp\left(\frac{\|\Delta_{t}\|^{2}}{2\sigma_{t}^{2}}\right)-1\right)\right]

where hk′=tk−tk−1′h^{\prime}_{k}=t_{k}-t^{\prime}_{k-1}. Now, applying Gronwall’s inequality will result in:

𝔼⁡[‖xtk−1′−x^tk−1′‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|x_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}-\hat{x}_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}\right\|^{2}\right] ≤exp⁡((2+2​d2​hk′σtk−1′4+2hk′)​hk′)​(∫tk−1′tkhk′​εs​c​o​r​e2​𝑑t)\displaystyle\leq\exp\left(\left(2+\frac{2d^{2}h^{\prime}_{k}}{\sigma_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}^{4}}+\frac{2}{h^{\prime}_{k}}\right)h^{\prime}_{k}\right)\left(\int_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}^{t_{k}}h^{\prime}_{k}\,\varepsilon^{2}_{score}dt\right)\quad

The exponential part is given by:

For large dd, the dominant term in the exponential is 2​d2​hk′2σtk−1′4\frac{2d^{2}h^{\prime 2}_{k}}{\sigma_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}^{4}}. If hk′2h^{\prime 2}_{k} does not decay sufficiently with d2σtk−1′4\frac{d^{2}}{\sigma_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}^{4}}, this term grows very rapidly. and thus, the overall term is of the order O⁡(σtk−1′4​εs​c​o​r​e2d2){O}(\frac{\sigma_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}^{4}\varepsilon^{2}_{score}}{d^{2}}).

Substituting this into the sum in Lemma A.2, we get:

𝔼pt1,..,tK[∑k=1KKL(pk−1|k(⋅|𝐱k)∥p^k−1|k(⋅|𝐱k))]=∑k=1Ke2​(tk′−tk)2​(1−e2​(tk′−tk))𝔼pt1,..,tK∥f(tk′,tk,𝐱k)−f^(tk′,tk,𝐱k)∥22.\mathbb{E}_{{p}_{t_{1},..,t_{K}}}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{KL}\left({p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\big\|\hat{p}_{k-1|k}(\cdot|{{\mathbf{x}}}_{k})\right)\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{e^{2(t_{k}^{\prime}-t_{k})}}{2(1-e^{2(t_{k}^{\prime}-t_{k})})}\mathbb{E}_{{p}_{t_{1},..,t_{K}}}\|f(t_{k}^{\prime},t_{k},{\mathbf{x}}_{k})-\hat{f}(t_{k}^{\prime},t_{k},{\mathbf{x}}_{k})\|_{2}^{2}.

when hk<hk′<σtk−1′2dh_{k}<h^{\prime}_{k}<\frac{\sigma^{2}_{t^{\prime}_{k-1}}}{d}. Let us denote the upper bound on this term as Q=e4​h′k2​εs​c​o​r​e2Q=e^{4}{h^{\prime}}_{k}^{2}\varepsilon^{2}_{score} for all kk.

Lemma C.1.

Assuming the exponential integrator as the ODE solver ϕ\phi for the consistency distillation training with some discretization {tn}n∈[1,N]\{t_{n}\}_{n\in[1,N]}, we have

𝔼q^​[‖𝐱^tn−1ϕ−𝐱^tn−1‖22]=O~​(ehn−1​L3​hn−12​d)\mathbb{E}_{\hat{q}}[\|\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n-1}}-\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{n-1}}\|^{2}_{2}]=\tilde{O}(e^{h_{n-1}}L^{3}h_{n-1}^{2}d)

where 𝐱^tn−1ϕ\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n-1}} is a step from 𝐱^tn\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{n}} using Φ\Phi, i.e. 𝐱^tn−1ϕ=𝐱^tn−1−(tn−tn−1)​s^tn​(xtn)\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n-1}}=\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{n-1}}-(t_{n}-t_{n-1})\hat{s}_{t_{n}}(x_{t_{n}}), dd is the dimension, hn−1=tn−tn−1h_{n-1}=t_{n}-t_{n-1} and 𝐱^tn−1\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t_{n-1}} corresponds to the ODE:

Proof.

Since, y^tn−1ϕ\hat{y}^{\phi}_{t_{n-1}} is just exponential integrator type discretization on the score function applied to the empirical PF ODE (eq. 6), it will follow the ODE:

Now, we denote et=𝐱^tϕ−𝐱^te_{t}=\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t}^{\phi}-\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t} and for t∈[tn−1,tn]t\in[t_{n-1},t_{n}] we have the corresponding ODE for its evolution as:

d​etd​t=(et+𝒔^tn​(𝐱^tnϕ)−𝒔^t​(𝐱^t))\frac{de_{t}}{dt}=\left(e_{t}+\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t_{n}}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n}})-\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})\right)

Now, we have to bound: T1≤‖et‖22T_{1}\leq\|e_{t}\|^{2}_{2}. We have:

d​‖et‖22d​t=2​⟨et,d​etd​t⟩=2​‖et‖22+2​⟨et,et+𝒔^tn​(y^tnϕ)−𝒔^t​(𝐱^t)⟩\frac{d\|e_{t}\|^{2}_{2}}{dt}=2\langle e_{t},\frac{de_{t}}{dt}\rangle=2\|e_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+2\langle e_{t},e_{t}+\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t_{n}}(\hat{y}^{\phi}_{t_{n}})-\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})\rangle

Now, applying cauchy schwartz in the second term (⟨a,b⟩≤‖a‖​‖b‖\langle a,b\rangle\leq\|a\|\|b\|) and then using 2​a​b≤a2+b22ab\leq a^{2}+b^{2}:

d​‖et‖22d​t≤2​‖et‖22+2​‖et‖2​‖𝒔^tn​(𝐱^tnϕ)−𝒔^t​(𝐱^t)‖2≤‖et‖22+‖et+𝒔^tn​(𝐱^tnϕ)−𝒔^t​(𝐱^t)‖22\frac{d\|e_{t}\|^{2}_{2}}{dt}\leq 2\|e_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+2\|e_{t}\|_{2}\|\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t_{n}}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n}})-\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})\|_{2}\leq\|e_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+\|e_{t}+\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t_{n}}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n}})-\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})\|^{2}_{2}

Now, we can observe the following form here: u′​(t)≤β⁡(t)​u​(t)+α⁡(t)u^{\prime}(t)\leq\beta(t)u(t)+\alpha(t) and using the gronwall inequality, we will now have u⁡(t)≤u⁡(t0)​e(∫β⁡(s)​𝑑s)+∫α⁡(s)​e∫β⁡(r)​𝑑r​𝑑su(t)\leq u(t_{0})e^{(\int\beta(s)ds)}+\int\alpha(s)e^{\int\beta(r)dr}ds. Utilizing this into the above equation, we have:

𝔼pt1,…,tN​[‖𝐱^n−1ϕ−𝐱n−1‖22]≤ehn−1​∫tn−1tn𝔼pt1,…,tN​[‖𝒔^tn​(𝐱^tnϕ)−𝒔^t​(𝐱^t)‖22]​𝑑t\mathbb{E}_{p_{t_{1},...,t_{N}}}\left[\|\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{n-1}-{\mathbf{x}}_{n-1}\|^{2}_{2}\right]\leq e^{h_{n-1}}\int_{t_{n-1}}^{t_{n}}\mathbb{E}_{p_{t_{1},...,t_{N}}}\left[\|\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t_{n}}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n}})-\hat{{\bm{s}}}_{t}(\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}_{t})\|^{2}_{2}\right]dt

where we denote tn−tn−1=hn−1t_{n}-t_{n-1}=h_{n-1}. Now, using the smoothness of the estimated score function, we have: Thus, we have:

Proof of Theorem 3.5.

Given the above lemmas, we now provide the proof of Theorem 3.5 mentioned in the main paper regarding bounding the error between actual f^\hat{f} and its estimated version f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta}.

Proof.

For any tN=αt_{N}=\alpha, we know that f^θ(α,α,⋅)=f^(α,⋅,⋅)\hat{f}_{\theta}(\alpha,\alpha,\cdot)=\hat{f}(\alpha,\cdot,\cdot) which we can construct via design. Thus, we can rewrite it as: 𝔼q​‖f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1′,𝐱n−1′)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tn,𝐱n)‖22\mathbb{E}_{q}\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t^{\prime}_{n-1},{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\prime}_{n-1})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n})\|_{2}^{2}. Thus, we have:

=𝔼pt1,…,tN​‖f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1′,𝐱n−1′)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tk,𝐱n)‖22\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{t_{1},...,t_{N}}}\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t^{\prime}_{n-1},{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\prime}_{n-1})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{k},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n})\|_{2}^{2}
=𝔼pt1,…,tN​‖f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1′,𝐱n−1′)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1,𝐱^n−1ϕ)+f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1,𝐱^n−1ϕ)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tn,𝐱n)‖22\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{t_{1},...,t_{N}}}\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t^{\prime}_{n-1},{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\prime}_{n-1})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n-1},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{n-1})+\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n-1},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{n-1})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n})\|_{2}^{2}

where ytnϕy^{\phi}_{t_{n}} implies taking a step via the given ODE solver at time tnt_{n}. Proof of Theorem 3.7.

Given the above lemmas and their proofs, we now provide the proof of Theorem 3.7 mentioned in the main paper regarding bounding the error between actual f{f} and its estimated version f^θ\hat{f}_{\theta} for the non-smooth score scenario. Here we will utilize the Lemma 3.6 and Lemma C.1 to bound the error.

Proof.

For any tN=αt_{N}=\alpha, we know that f^θ(α,α,⋅)=f^(α,⋅,⋅)\hat{f}_{\theta}(\alpha,\alpha,\cdot)=\hat{f}(\alpha,\cdot,\cdot) which we can construct via design. Thus, we have:

=𝔼pt1,..,tK​‖f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1′,𝐱n−1′)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tn,𝐱n)‖22\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{t_{1},..,t_{K}}}\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t^{\prime}_{n-1},{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\prime}_{n-1})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n})\|_{2}^{2}
=𝔼pt1,..,tK​‖f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1′,𝐱n−1′)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1,𝐱^n−1ϕ)+f^θ​(tn−1′,tn−1,𝐱^n−1ϕ)−f^θ​(tn−1′,tn,𝐱n)‖22\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{p_{t_{1},..,t_{K}}}\|\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t^{\prime}_{n-1},{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\prime}_{n-1})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n-1},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{n-1})+\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n-1},\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{n-1})-\hat{f}_{\theta}(t^{\prime}_{n-1},t_{n},{{\mathbf{x}}}_{n})\|_{2}^{2}

where 𝐱^tnϕ\hat{{\mathbf{x}}}^{\phi}_{t_{n}} implies taking a step via the given ODE solver at time tnt_{n}.
